source.title: Benchmarking Deep AUROC Optimization: Loss Functions and Algorithmic Choices
source.authors: Dixian Zhu; Xiaodong Wu; Tian-Bao Yang

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly compares optimizer, regularization, and output-normalization choices and reports testing AUROC results. It refines the optimizer claim: Adam-style optimizers can converge faster on training loss but do not show better testing performance in the tested settings. It does not measure train–test error gaps, random-label memorization, architecture comparisons, or width scaling.
record.gate_note: Rows capture results from the paper's own testing-AUROC comparisons of algorithmic choices. Training-loss convergence curves are summarized in the paper but not given numerical values in the text; they are not separate rows. Claims cited from prior studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4 in a new setting: deep binary image classification trained for AUROC, comparing adaptive and nonadaptive optimizers with learning-rate tuning. Held-out AUROC directly measures the performance named by V4; a train–test error gap is not required. Molecular graph tasks fall outside the image and language systems specified by V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: Adam-type optimizers are competitive in training convergence but generally worse in validation and testing; oversampling and suitable output normalization help, and regularization choices depend on the dataset. Their conclusion is an aggregate tendency, not a universal ordering: Table 7 contains Adam wins. The training curves use CSH, while Table 7 evaluates PSQ and CSQ.
record.recipe_differences: The paper benchmarks deep AUROC objectives and algorithmic choices using testing AUROC rather than training–test error gaps; it does not test the original claim's random-label, width, architecture, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Testing AUROC varies with dataset, objective (PSQ or CSQ), optimizer, positive sampling rate, consecutive epoch regularization, weight decay, and output activation/normalization. The paper notes large CER can degrade performance on highly imbalanced MUV and ToxCast(t12); Adam-style optimizer outcomes also vary by dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimizer rankings vary across molecular graph tasks: Adam trails both comparators in several settings, beats both in others, and sometimes lies between them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizer performance in molecular graph AUROC prediction depends on the dataset and objective.

fits_no_version.finding: Sigmoid output improves CIFAR10 test AUROC over no output activation for PSQ and CSQ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output activation can improve held-out AUROC in deep AUROC optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: PSQ CIFAR10 AUROC is 0.907 with either zero or 1e-4 weight decay and 0.911 with 1e-3 weight decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-decay strength can affect held-out AUROC independently of dropout and optimizer comparisons.

record.problems: The authors state that they did not exhaustively search all algorithmic settings because of computational cost. The principal reported metric is testing AUROC, so these comparisons do not directly measure a training–test error gap. The text reports means and standard deviations but no significance tests.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional per-dataset results for sampling rate, consecutive epoch regularization, weight decay, output normalization, and loss-function comparisons in Tables 4–6 and 9–19. They are omitted because these algorithmic-choice comparisons do not establish train–test error gaps or fit the named optimizer version as directly as Table 7; Table 7 rows include the per-dataset PSQ/CSQ optimizer comparisons and are within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label fitting and corresponding held-out evaluation.
No width sweep, zero-training-error threshold, or post-threshold test-error comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture or locality comparison.

No language benchmarks, controlled comparison of limited versus broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, or Adam-to-SGD switching. Training convergence uses CSH, whereas the optimizer test-AUROC table uses PSQ and CSQ, so equal or better training performance and worse test performance are not established for matched objectives. Margin parameters and evaluation stopping points are also selected, so the protocol is not literally learning-rate-and-schedule-only tuning.
Batch size remains 64; no large-batch comparison or compensating recipe.
No dropout intervention or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison with generalization gaps.
No memorization-based example removal and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 7 values match the supplied text. Parentheses report standard deviations, not significance tests. PSQ uses standard optimizer types; CSQ uses compositional variants. The optimizer subsection states CER=0.002 for all datasets, although preceding tuning sections retain CER=0 for molecular tasks, leaving that molecular condition internally ambiguous. The normalization and weight-decay experiments are valid results but do not test the supplied versions.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-label test performance is measured, but the paper does not train on random labels or evaluate random-label test accuracy.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or locality intervention.

Tests SGD-style, Momentum-style, and Adam-style methods on AUROC tasks, not the image-classification and language benchmark suite in the version; does not test broad hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, or switching from Adam to SGD.
No sharpness, perturbation, norm, or margin measurement.

relationships.condition: PSQ and CSQ on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Cat vs Dog; CSQ on STL10 and Cardiomegaly
relationships.reason: R4–R11 and R15 show lower mean test AUROC for Adam than both SGD and Momentum under the tested tuning protocol.
relationships.display_finding: The reported lower mean test AUROC for Adam than both SGD and Momentum remains unverified.

relationships.condition: PSQ on STL10 and CSQ on Melanoma
relationships.reason: R1–R3 and R13 show comparator dependence: Adam beats SGD but trails Momentum.
relationships.display_finding: Adam reportedly exceeded plain SGD but trailed Momentum, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.reason: R12 and R14 show slightly higher mean AUROC for Adam than both comparators, without significance tests; these are exceptions to the overall tendency.
relationships.display_finding: Adam reportedly achieved slightly higher mean AUROC than both comparators, but these results remain unverified and significance was untested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: PSQ and CSQ on most tested datasets
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that Adam-type methods have worse testing performance than Momentum and SGD in its benchmark; R6–R11, R15–R23, and R25 show lower or mixed Adam-style AUROC in many settings.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Adam-style testing AUROC exceeds both comparators for some PSQ/CSQ dataset settings; on Melanoma CSQ and ToxCast(t8) CSQ it beats one comparator, so the pattern is not universal (R12–R14, R24–R27).
